title: Wangari Maathai and the Seedlings Women Were Paid to Keep Alive
dek: On World Environment Day 1977 a Nairobi scientist planted a handful of seedlings, then chose to pay rural women to grow and tend their own.

story.event: The first planting on World Environment Day 1977 and the decision to pay women for seedlings they raised
story.summary: Working through the National Council of Women of Kenya, Wangari Maathai began the Green Belt Movement with a small planting on World Environment Day, 5 June 1977. When free seedlings from the Forestry Department ran short and foresters prepared to charge for them, the women learned to grow their own, and the movement paid them for seedlings they raised successfully, funded first by companies and then by a $100,000 grant from the fund that became UNIFEM. By the early 1980s there were about 600 nurseries and 2,000 public green belts.
paragraphs: In 1976 Wangari Maathai became head of veterinary anatomy at the University of Nairobi, the first woman in East and Central Africa to chair a university department. That year she was also active in the National Council of Women of Kenya, and there she put forward the idea of planting trees with ordinary people. Rural women had told her what they lacked: firewood, clean drinking water, a balanced diet, shelter and income. "I don't know why I picked on a tree," she told a university audience in 2007, but it was easy to explain.

The first planting was small. The movement's own account says it began with seven seedlings on World Environment Day, 5 June 1977; the Nobel Committee's chairman, presenting her prize in 2004, spoke of nine trees in her backyard. Soon rows of about a thousand seedlings were going in to make public green belts. Maathai asked Kenya's chief forester for 15 million seedlings, one for every Kenyan, and at first he agreed. But the women collected them faster than expected, and foresters were about to start charging.

Maathai knew that earlier tree programmes had failed because people planted and walked away. So the women would grow their own seedlings, and the movement would pay them for the ones they raised successfully, so that the care did not stop at planting. Nobody trained them as foresters; they taught one another, using what they knew from growing food. "We became independent of foresters," she said. The early money came from companies including Mobil Oil, then a $100,000 grant from the fund that became UNIFEM, "more money than we had ever seen in our lives."

Not everything took. Her memoir recalls a first nursery whose trees were killed by drought. But by the early 1980s there were about 600 nurseries involving 2,000 to 3,000 women, and some 2,000 public green belts. The totals grew with the years and depend on who was counting: more than 20 million trees by 1993, by the women's own reports; over 30 million by her Nobel lecture in 2004; more than 51 million by the movement's count in 2017.

quote.connection: In Saadi's tale, district officials say this while planning to destroy a band of raiders before they grow strong. Read from the other side, it is Maathai's insight: a seedling is easiest to lose in its first months, which is why she paid for trees that lived, not trees that went into the ground.

reflection: Maathai's quiet decision was about what to count. Planting a seedling takes an afternoon; keeping it alive takes months of watering that nobody sees. By paying for the trees that lived, she made the unseen part of the work the part that was rewarded.

You probably measure some of your own days by what you started: messages sent, tasks opened, plans drafted. Those are easy to count and easy to feel busy about. It may be worth asking which of last month's beginnings are still alive, and giving those your attention before you plant anything new.
invitation: Pick one thing you started in the past month. Check whether it is still alive, and if it is, give it twenty minutes of care today instead of beginning something new.

cross_checks.claim: Maathai began the Green Belt Movement in 1977 through the National Council of Women of Kenya, having introduced the idea there in 1976.
The first planting took place on World Environment Day, 5 June 1977 (seven seedlings by the movement's account, nine trees by the Nobel Committee chairman's).
Rural women's needs for firewood, clean water, food and income prompted the tree planting.
Women grew their own seedlings and were paid for those they raised (selling seedlings to the movement).
United Nations funding helped the idea grow.
More than 20 million trees had been planted by the early 1990s, and over 30 million by 2004.

research_notes: The first planting is told differently. The Green Belt Movement's own guest post on the Goldman Prize site says it began with seven seedlings on World Environment Day 1977; the Nobel Committee chairman's 2004 presentation speech says she planted nine trees in her backyard on 5 June 1977 (the Goldman Prize's profile also mentions a small backyard nursery). Several secondary accounts, citing her memoir Unbowed, place the seven trees in Kamukunji Park in Nairobi after a procession organised by the National Council of Women; those pages were blocked or dead for the verifier, so the park is not named and the story gives both versions, with who said what. The same presentation speech says she resigned her university chair in 1977; the Nobel biography instead records her becoming associate professor that year, so the story does not mention a resignation. Payment: the UB Reporter paraphrases her as compensating women for successfully nurturing seedlings, and the Right Livelihood Foundation says women's groups sold millions of seedlings to the movement; no payment amount was found in a loading source, so none is given. Tree totals disagree by date and counter: more than 20 million (Right Livelihood, by the women's own reports to the end of 1993; the Nobel biography; the Goldman profile), about 30 million (her 2004 Nobel lecture, the presentation speech, the UB Reporter in 2007) and more than 51 million (the movement in 2017); the story gives each with its date and source rather than one figure. The 15 million seedlings asked of the chief forester comes from the UB Reporter's paraphrase of her 2007 lecture. The drought that killed her first nursery comes from America Magazine's review of her memoir and is attributed to the memoir. The Saadi passage is spoken by officials planning to uproot a band of robbers; the connection applies it by contrast.
